messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When his four-year-old daughter was admitted to the hospital with a sudden, life-threatening infection during a week of cold rain, Lukas Meyer felt as if the world had narrowed to fluorescent lights, monitor alarms, and the sight of her small body in a bed that looked too large for her. He remembered standing by the window watching sleet stripe the glass while doctors moved quickly around her, and the clearest parts of the ordeal stayed with him as sharp visual fragments: her gray face under the hospital blanket, the tubing taped to her hand, his wife crying into her coat sleeve. Even now, those moments came back mostly as pictures, precise and bright. At the same time, he rarely let the memory run to the end. As soon as he began to get close to the worst part—waiting to hear whether she would survive—he would mentally shove it away, as if completing the sequence might make it happen again.

In the months after his daughter recovered, Lukas did not feel relieved in the way he had expected. He had come to believe that a decent father should have protected his child before she ever became critically ill, and in his mind he had failed in the most basic duty. That judgment spread beyond the event itself. Once he had decided that he was the kind of father who missed signs and failed to keep his child safe, ordinary cues stopped feeling neutral to him. News about illness, cold rain on the windows, or the sound of a child coughing caught and held his attention because each of them seemed like possible proof that danger had been there before he noticed it. He told his wife that he no longer recognized himself and, in quieter moments, felt he had become someone hollowed out and unfamiliar, a man organized around fear rather than competence. Those beliefs made the hospital images feel charged and unbearable; when they surfaced, they seemed to prove what he thought about himself. A glimpse in his mind of his daughter’s hand under the blanket could quickly become evidence that he had failed her, and because of that he cut the memory short before he could fully recall it.

Lukas worked as a financial analyst in a downtown office where muted televisions in the lobby and on the trading floor often carried breaking news. A report about pediatric illness, a segment about children’s hospitals, even a general health scare was enough to make his body react before he had thought anything through. He would scan the room, notice exits, and feel unable to settle until he had identified how he would get out quickly if something went wrong. Rainy, gray weather had a similar effect; on stormy mornings he arrived at work already tense, and if he passed a family with young children in the elevator, he felt a jolt of alarm that made no objective sense to him and yet felt completely real. In those moments the reminder did not stay a reminder; it turned the present into something dangerous, as if the emergency were already beginning again around him. A weather forecast or the sight of a child with a cough could fill him with the same immediate certainty that something terrible was about to happen. Those moments also brought a punishing thought with them: other fathers could stand near children or hear difficult news without unraveling, whereas he was apparently the kind of man who had failed once and remained incapable of keeping anyone safe.

Over time, his own watchfulness widened the field of what felt dangerous. Because he was so quick to react, he became increasingly attentive to anything that might set him off—screens in waiting rooms, weather apps forecasting cold rain, the sound of children coughing in restaurants. He checked exits in movie theaters, conference rooms, and even at his daughter’s preschool events before he could relax enough to sit down. Nights became particularly difficult. Living in that state of danger made the world feel crowded with warnings he could not easily dismiss. Already braced for catastrophe, he found that more and more things registered as reminders—the glow of a hospital ad on a screen, a damp coat in the office elevator, a parent mentioning a fever at preschool pickup. He lay awake convinced he needed to stay alert, as if sleeping too deeply would mean missing the next catastrophe. In that state of constant readiness, the images of the hospital returned more easily: the monitor, the blanket, the window streaked with bad weather. Once those images intruded, he noticed even more acutely the kinds of cues that resembled them in daily life, so that a rainy commute or a headline on his phone could feel loaded before he had consciously registered why.

The memories themselves also seemed to teach him what to fear. Because they were so visual and exact, ordinary cues acquired the force of direct reminders rather than distant associations. A child’s pale face in a grocery store line, a weather report predicting sleet, a news anchor mentioning ICU capacity could pull him toward the same set of images, and he had begun to organize his days around avoiding that pull. He muted office televisions when he could, changed routes to avoid the pediatric wing near the hospital where his daughter had been treated, and sometimes asked his wife to take their daughter to birthday parties because being around groups of children left him too activated to think clearly.

By the time Lukas sought help, his marriage had begun to feel strained by how much his life revolved around vigilance. His wife saw that he was present physically but rarely at ease, and he knew she missed the man he had once been. What finally brought him in was a recent evening when rain started unexpectedly during his daughter’s soccer practice. Surrounded by children in wet jackets, he felt the old images slam back so vividly that he began planning how to leave the field, where the nearest exit was, and how fast they could get to the car. Looking at the other parents, he was seized again by the conviction that he had become unrecognizable to himself. He wanted help because he was terrified that this was now permanent—that every storm, every news alert, every child-filled room would keep proving he had failed and keep him braced for a disaster that was not actually happening.
